objectives: Compute carrier statistics in doped semiconductors.
Analyze p-n junctions, BJTs, and MOSFETs from band-bending physics.

slides.title: Doping, carrier statistics, and the Fermi level
slides.body:
Semiconductors are insulators with band gaps small enough that thermal excitation, doping, or photons can produce useful carrier densities. Si dominates electronics; GaAs, InP, GaN, SiC dominate optoelectronics + power. The semiconductor industry is built on band engineering.

**Intrinsic carrier density** in an undoped, perfect semiconductor:

$$n_i = \sqrt{N_c N_v}\; e^{-E_g/2k_BT}$$

with effective DOS $N_c = 2(m_e^* k_B T/2\pi\hbar^2)^{3/2}$, similarly $N_v$ for holes. For Si at 300 K, $n_i \approx 10^{10}$ cm$^{-3}$ — extremely small relative to the atomic density ~ $5 \times 10^{22}$ cm$^{-3}$. Pure Si is essentially insulating.

**Mass action law**: $np = n_i^2$ at thermal equilibrium, regardless of doping.

**Doping**:
- **Donor** (n-type): substituting Si by P, As, Sb adds one extra electron loosely bound by hydrogenic Coulomb attraction with effective dielectric constant $\varepsilon_r \sim 11.7$ + effective mass $m_e^* \sim 0.26 m_e$ for Si. Binding energy $E_D \sim 45$ meV — ionized at room temperature.
- **Acceptor** (p-type): B, Al, Ga, In create holes; binding $\sim 45$ meV for B in Si.
- Modulation doping (Esaki + Tsu 1969; Dingle 1978) puts dopants in barrier layers + carriers in clean wells → ultra-high mobility 2DEGs in GaAs/AlGaAs (the platform for fractional quantum Hall).
- **Compensation, deep levels (DX centers), self-compensation**: complicate p-doping in wide-gap materials (GaN, ZnO, diamond — long-standing materials challenge).

**Fermi level**:
- Intrinsic: $E_F$ near midgap (slight shift from $m_e^* \neq m_h^*$).
- n-type (heavy): $E_F$ near $E_c$ (conduction-band edge); degenerate if $E_F > E_c$.
- p-type: $E_F$ near $E_v$.

**Mobility + transport**:
- Drift: $J = \sigma E$ with $\sigma = ne\mu_e + pe\mu_h$.
- Si at 300 K: $\mu_e \approx 1400$, $\mu_h \approx 450$ cm²/V·s. GaAs $\mu_e \approx 8500$; InSb $\mu_e \approx 80000$.
- Scattering: phonons (room-T limit), ionized impurities (low-T limit), surface roughness in MOSFETs, alloy disorder in ternaries.
- Diffusion: $J = eD \nabla n$; Einstein relation $D = (k_B T/e)\mu$.
- Hall measurement: sign + magnitude → carrier type + density.

**Optical excitation + recombination**:
- Direct gap: photon $\hbar\omega > E_g$ creates electron-hole pair vertically in $\mathbf{k}$.
- Indirect gap: phonon-assisted; weak absorption + radiative emission.
- Recombination paths: radiative (LEDs, lasers), Auger (3-body, dominant at high carrier density — kills LED efficiency at high current), Shockley-Read-Hall (defect-mediated, dominant at low injection).

slides.title: p-n junctions, diodes, BJTs, and MOSFETs
slides.body:
**p-n junction** — the building block of every semiconductor device. Joining p- and n-type Si causes carriers to diffuse + recombine, leaving ionized dopants → **depletion region** with electric field opposing further diffusion. At equilibrium, $E_F$ is flat across the junction; bands bend by built-in potential $V_{bi} = (k_B T/e) \ln(N_A N_D/n_i^2) \sim 0.7$ V for moderately doped Si.

**Shockley diode equation** (William Shockley 1949):

$$I = I_0 \big(e^{eV/k_BT} - 1\big).$$

- Forward bias: barrier lowered; injected minority carriers diffuse + recombine → exponential current.
- Reverse bias: small saturation current $I_0$ + breakdown above critical field (avalanche, Zener — used in voltage references, ESD protection).
- $I_0$ depends on minority-carrier diffusion lengths + lifetimes.

**Bipolar Junction Transistor (BJT)** (Bardeen + Brattain + Shockley 1947, Nobel 1956 — invention of the transistor; replaced vacuum tubes within a decade; foundation of modern electronics):
- Two back-to-back junctions: npn or pnp.
- Base region is thin compared to minority diffusion length → carriers injected from emitter cross to collector.
- Current gain $\beta = I_C/I_B \sim 100-1000$.
- Workhorse for analog + high-speed RF + power amplifiers; SiGe HBTs go to >100 GHz.

**MOSFET (Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor Field-Effect Transistor)** — the dominant device of modern electronics (Atalla + Kahng 1959 at Bell Labs; >$10^{22}$ MOSFETs manufactured to date).
- Gate over thin oxide (SiO₂ or high-κ HfO₂ in modern nodes) over Si channel.
- Gate bias modulates surface carrier density (inversion layer) → controls current between source + drain.
- **Threshold voltage** $V_T$: depends on doping, oxide thickness, work function.
- **Subthreshold swing**: minimum $S = (k_B T/e)\ln 10 \approx 60$ mV/decade — fundamental thermal limit, motivates beyond-CMOS research (tunnel FETs, NCFETs, spin FETs).
- **Scaling**: Dennard (1974) — voltage + size scale together. Moore's law (1965, 1975): transistors per chip doubled every ~18-24 months. From planar bulk → SOI → strained Si → FinFET (Hu 1999; manufactured by Intel 2011, TSMC + Samsung) → Gate-All-Around / nanosheet (Samsung 3nm 2022, TSMC 2nm 2025) → 2D-channel + monolithic 3D research.
- Modern node: TSMC N3, N2 with EUV lithography; ~10$^{10}$ transistors per chip (Apple M3 Max ~92B); contact gate pitch ~45 nm; transistor density ~200 MTr/mm².

**Power devices**:
- IGBT (insulated-gate bipolar transistor): hybrid for ~kV / kA.
- SiC + GaN power FETs: wide-gap → higher breakdown field + temperature + efficiency. Tesla Model 3 inverter switched to SiC MOSFETs (2017) — 5% range gain. EV chargers, datacenter PSUs, RF amps for 5G + 6G.

**Memory**:
- DRAM: 1T1C cell, refresh.
- Flash (NAND + NOR): floating-gate (Kahng + Sze 1967) → 3D NAND (Samsung 2013; now >200 layers, V-NAND).
- Emerging: MRAM, PCRAM, ReRAM, FeRAM.

**Beyond silicon**: SiGe channels for strain + mobility; III-V channels (InGaAs) for n-MOSFETs; Ge for p-MOSFETs; 2D channels (MoS₂, WSe₂) as candidates for ultra-scaled gates.

slides.title: Optoelectronics, wide-bandgap, and 2D materials
slides.body:
**LEDs (light-emitting diodes)**:
- Forward-biased p-n junction radiatively recombines injected carriers.
- Direct-gap materials: AlGaInP for red/orange, InGaN for green/blue/UV. Red GaAsP (Holonyak 1962), blue InGaN (Akasaki + Amano + Nakamura, Nobel 2014).
- White LEDs: blue InGaN + Ce:YAG phosphor. Now ~200 lm/W wall-plug → revolutionized lighting (10× efficiency of incandescent). Lighting accounts for ~6% of global electricity; LED transition is a major decarbonization win.

**Laser diodes**:
- Population inversion + optical resonator (Fabry-Pérot, DFB, DBR, VCSEL).
- Threshold current $J_{th}$; above threshold, stimulated emission dominates.
- Wavelengths: 405 nm (Blu-ray), 650 nm (DVD), 850/980/1310/1550 nm (telecom), 9.6 μm CO₂ (EUV plasma drive at ASML).
- Quantum-well + quantum-dot active regions reduce threshold + improve gain.
- VCSELs for iPhone Face ID, datacenter optics.

**Photovoltaics**:
- Si single-junction efficiency record 26.8% (LONGi 2023); Shockley-Queisser limit ~33% for single junction.
- Multijunction GaInP/GaAs/Ge tandems: >47% under concentration (NREL); used in spacecraft + concentrator PV.
- **Perovskite solar cells**: methylammonium lead halide (MAPbI₃) discovered Miyasaka 2009 → 26% efficiency by 2024; tandem with Si reaches >34% (Oxford PV 2024). Stability, lead toxicity, large-area manufacturing still challenges.
- Organic + dye-sensitized + CIGS + CdTe + thin-film alternatives.

**Wide-bandgap semiconductors**:
- **GaN** ($E_g$ = 3.4 eV): blue LEDs, lasers, RF power, EVs, datacenters. The Nobel 2014 InGaN blue LED transformed lighting.
- **SiC** ($E_g$ = 3.26 eV): power MOSFETs, Schottky diodes — replacing Si in EV inverters + onboard chargers.
- **Ga₂O₃** ($E_g$ = 4.8 eV, ultrawide): emerging for ultra-high-voltage power.
- **Diamond** ($E_g$ = 5.5 eV): research; doping remains hard.
- **AlN, BN, β-Ga₂O₃**: deep-UV LEDs for disinfection, water purification.

**III-V high-mobility + heterostructures**:
- GaAs/AlGaAs 2DEGs: mobility >$10^7$ cm²/V·s; platform for FQHE experiments (Tsui, Stormer, Laughlin Nobel 1998), Aharonov-Bohm interferometry, anyonic statistics tests.
- InAs/GaSb: 2D topological insulator candidate.
- HEMT (high-electron-mobility transistor): GaN HEMTs in 5G base stations, satellite, military radar.

**2D materials**:
- **Graphene** (Geim + Novoselov 2004, Nobel 2010): zero-gap semimetal; Dirac cones at K + K'; very high mobility (>200000 cm²/V·s suspended at 4 K). No bandgap → poor switching but great RF + sensors.
- **Transition-metal dichalcogenides (TMDs)** — MoS₂, WS₂, WSe₂, MoTe₂: monolayers are direct-gap semiconductors (1-2 eV); strong spin-valley coupling; excitons with huge binding ~500 meV; field-effect transistors with subthreshold ~60 mV/dec.
- **Black phosphorus, h-BN, MXenes**.
- **Van der Waals heterostructures**: stack any 2D materials; engineer band alignments, moiré superlattices, twisted bilayer graphene magic angle (Cao + Jarillo-Herrero 2018) → flat bands + superconductivity + correlated insulators.

**Frontier**:
- Spin-FETs + Datta-Das transistor.
- Negative-capacitance FETs (Salahuddin 2008).
- Tunnel FETs to beat 60 mV/dec.
- Neuromorphic devices (memristors, PCM, ECRAM).
- Cryo-CMOS for quantum-computer control.
- 3D-monolithic CMOS integration.

**Industry**: Semiconductor revenue ~$600B (2024). Foundries (TSMC, Samsung, Intel, SMIC); IDMs (Intel, Samsung); fabless (NVIDIA, AMD, Qualcomm, Apple, Broadcom); EDA (Cadence, Synopsys, Siemens EDA); equipment (ASML EUV monopoly, Applied Materials, Lam, KLA). AI accelerators (NVIDIA H100, B100, Google TPU, AWS Trainium) drove the 2023-25 boom.

question.question: Derive the built-in potential of a p-n junction.
question.goal: For a p-n junction with acceptor density $N_A$ on the p-side + donor density $N_D$ on the n-side, derive $V_{bi} = (k_B T/e) \ln(N_A N_D/n_i^2)$.

steps.prompt: At equilibrium, what condition holds for the Fermi level across the junction?
hints: No net current → no electrochemical-potential gradient.
steps.reveal: At equilibrium, the Fermi level $E_F$ is constant throughout the junction — no electrochemical-potential gradient means no net diffusion or drift current.

steps.prompt: Express the bulk electron density $n$ in terms of $E_F$ and the conduction band edge $E_c$ in the n-region, and similarly the hole density $p$ in the p-region in terms of the valence-band edge $E_v$.

acceptedAnswers: n = N_c exp(-(E_c - E_F)/k_B T); p = N_v exp(-(E_F - E_v)/k_B T)

hints: Use the standard Boltzmann tails of the Fermi-Dirac distribution far from $E_F$.
steps.reveal: On the n-side: $n_n = N_c\, e^{-(E_c^n - E_F)/k_BT} \approx N_D$. On the p-side: $p_p = N_v\, e^{-(E_F - E_v^p)/k_BT} \approx N_A$.

steps.prompt: Express the built-in potential as the band-edge shift between the two regions.

acceptedAnswers: built-in potential equals the conduction band offset

hints: Bands bend by $eV_{bi}$ across the depletion region.
steps.reveal: Since $E_F$ is flat, the band edges shift by $eV_{bi}$ across the junction: $E_c^p - E_c^n = E_v^p - E_v^n = eV_{bi}$.

steps.prompt: Combine using mass action $n_p p_p = n_n p_n = n_i^2$ to express $V_{bi}$.

acceptedAnswers: V_bi = (k_B T / e) ln(N_A N_D / n_i^2)

steps.reveal: $n_n/n_p = N_D/(n_i^2/N_A) = N_A N_D/n_i^2$. But also $n_n/n_p = e^{eV_{bi}/k_BT}$ from Boltzmann + band bending. So $V_{bi} = (k_B T/e) \ln(N_A N_D/n_i^2)$. For Si with $N_A = N_D = 10^{17}$ cm$^{-3}$ + $n_i = 10^{10}$ cm$^{-3}$ at 300 K, $V_{bi} \approx 0.83$ V.

question.question: Why was the InGaN blue LED (Akasaki, Amano, Nakamura — Nobel 2014) such a historic breakthrough?
options: Efficient red + green LEDs existed since the 1960s-70s (Holonyak, AlGaInP), but blue/UV LEDs eluded researchers for ~30 years because no II-VI or III-V material with $E_g \sim 3$ eV could be p-doped effectively + lattice-matched + epitaxially grown defect-free. Akasaki + Amano (Nagoya) pioneered GaN MOCVD growth on sapphire with low-T buffer + Mg activation; Nakamura (Nichia) commercialized the InGaN/GaN double-heterostructure blue LED in 1993. With blue LEDs in hand, white LEDs became possible (blue + phosphor or RGB mixing). Lighting (~6% of global electricity) shifted to LEDs with 5-10× the efficacy of incandescent + 2× of fluorescent — a major decarbonization. Also enabled Blu-ray, full-color displays, plant lighting, UV disinfection. The 2014 Nobel cited 'invention of efficient blue light-emitting diodes which has enabled bright and energy-saving white light sources.'
question.explanation: Blue LEDs (Akasaki + Amano + Nakamura, Nobel 2014) ended a 30-year quest blocked by GaN growth + p-doping. Enabled white LEDs (blue + phosphor), revolutionized lighting (6% of global electricity, decarbonization), enabled Blu-ray, displays, UV disinfection.

hints: Why were red + green LEDs easy but blue hard?
slides.workedSolution: Blue LEDs (Akasaki + Amano + Nakamura, Nobel 2014) solved a 30-year materials problem: epitaxial GaN growth on sapphire + p-type Mg activation. Enabled white LEDs (blue + phosphor) → lighting revolution (6% of global electricity, 5-10× efficacy gain). Also: Blu-ray, full-color displays, UV disinfection.

question.question: Designing a SiC EV inverter
question.prompt: An EV traction inverter must switch 400-800 V DC at >100 kHz with low loss. Compare a 1200-V Si IGBT to a 1200-V SiC MOSFET on the relevant physics: critical breakdown field, on-resistance, switching loss, junction temperature limit, drive complexity, thermal management. Why did Tesla switch to SiC in 2017? What changes for next-generation 800 V SiC + GaN drivetrains?

question.question: Write the Shockley diode equation for current $I$ in terms of saturation current $I_0$, applied voltage $V$, and thermal voltage $k_B T/e$.
question.hint: Shockley 1949; exponential injection above turn-on, saturation $-I_0$ in reverse.

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain how doping + p-n junctions + MOSFETs underpin modern microelectronics and why wide-bandgap + 2D materials matter for the next era.
question.rubric: Mentions: doping (donors P/As, acceptors B/Al) shifts $E_F$, controls carrier density; mass action $np = n_i^2$; p-n junction band-bending + Shockley diode $I = I_0(e^{eV/kT}-1)$; BJT (Bardeen-Brattain-Shockley 1947, Nobel 1956) replaced vacuum tubes; MOSFET (Atalla-Kahng 1959) became dominant device after Dennard scaling + Moore's law (1965); modern nodes (FinFET → GAA nanosheet, 3 nm/2 nm, EUV); subthreshold limit 60 mV/dec drives beyond-CMOS research; SiC + GaN wide-gap for EV inverters + 5G + datacenters (Tesla switched to SiC 2017); InGaN blue LED (Nobel 2014) revolutionized lighting; perovskites for PV; 2D TMDs + graphene + twisted bilayer flat bands as future channels + correlated platforms; semiconductor industry ~$600B.
